summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: most Reels get 1,000+ views while the same videos on YouTube Shorts get under 60. The best performers use a 'X doesn't do the obvious thing, it only does Y' hook about a simple, familiar gadget (robot, clap switch, DHT11, mic). Later videos with plain 'How does X work?' titles and the YouTube-only uploads get almost no views, and the newest videos (Nov 14+) are dropping in reach.
winningPattern: Instagram Reels about a hands-on maker gadget (robot, clap switch, DHT11, mic, IR sensor) with a Hinglish 'myth-flip' hook: 'X doesn't do [obvious thing], it only does [surprising thing]'. Short punchy title with one emoji and #shorts. Robot and clap-switch topics lead on views/likes; shareable 'sunburn in clouds' and 'soil sensor' style myth-busters get the most shares (24-32) despite low views, so they have strong potential if the first seconds are improved. YouTube only worked for the earliest videos (Oct 29-Nov 5, ~400-680 views) and mostly for robot/clap topics.
doMore: Use the 'Doesn't do X, only does Y' contrarian hook in the title and first line on screen
Make more robot and clap-switch style videos with a visible, demo-able result (robot falls, switch reacts to whistle)
Post every video to Instagram Reels first and YouTube together, since YouTube-only videos get under 30 views
Turn high-share topics (UV, soil sensor) into a series with a stronger visual first 2 seconds and a 'send this to a friend' end line
End with a save-worthy tip (wiring or pin label) to lift saves, which were strong on the gyro and clap switch videos
stopDoing: Plain 'X Kaise Kaam Karta Hai?' question titles with no surprising claim
Publishing to only one platform (YouTube-only or English-only uploads)
Repeating near-identical topics like three tap/IR/clap variants within a week
